item.title: 7 Hardest SNES Games Nobody Could Beat
item.description:
For no reason at all, I love to punish myself with exceedingly difficult games . I tend to forgo joyful romps and low-cortisol cooking games for brutal, hair-pulling titles that get my heart rate rising. While there are a slew of difficult games available for all types of consoles, the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES) seems to have a few borderline infamous ones known for ruining gaming experiences and putting 90s kids and adults alike in a very bad mood.

Many older titles' intense difficulty is due to external factors often involving money. Gaming manufacturers made rentable games extremely tough to stretch their playthrough length. The difficulty prevented players from beating games in the span of a weekend, which meant once their rental had expired, they'd need to rent again, or buy the cartridge for themselves. This method got players hooked on the adrenaline of trying to beat the impossible, inadvertently putting money into game developers' pockets. Forget Soulslike titles or even Cuphead . These games might just be the worst of the worst. In no specific order, here are some of the hardest SNES games that seemingly nobody could beat.

8 Legendary SNES Games That Are 100% Unplayable Now

Don’t dust off your Super Nintendo for these legendary SNES titles. They may be iconic, but they are a struggle to get through today.

By Evan Regan

Super Ghouls 'N Ghosts

No Hand-Holding Here

Super Ghouls 'n Ghosts was released for the SNES back in 1991. As it stands today, the game is one of the hardest around. I'm talking "throwing the controller across the room" frustrating. This Capcom title is a side-scroller centered around Arthur , a brave knight who must rescue Princess Guinevere from the clutches of Emperor Sardius.

Many point to the jump mechanic as frustrating simply because it is impossible to master. Once players jump, they're locked into an arc and can't change course, meaning if an enemy suddenly decides to cross Arthur's path mid-jump, it'll collide with him no matter what. A double-jump mechanic was introduced, but that didn't seem to save players any grief.

The health system isn't easygoing either. Once Arthur is struck, he loses his armor, leaving him in his undies. A second hit kills the brave knight, turning him into a skeleton, causing players to lose a life. This is a way less forgiving system than your standard decremental health bar per hit.

6 Classic Horror Games That Are Difficult To Replay Nowadays

These iconic horror game classics were monumental for their time, but returning to them now is quit difficult due to their dated mechanics.

6
By Connor Wright

Through grit, determination, and likely lots of tears, once players reach the final boss, Emperor Sardius, the nightmare is not over. Far from it. Getting to this point likely took weeks upon weeks, a monumental victory, but instead of congratulating players on their accomplishments, they are told they must replay the game from the very beginning to obtain a weapon strong enough to defeat Sardius. This is a mandatory step, given that the item needed to successfully kill the Emperor, the Goddess Bracelet, is only available via a second playthrough.

The Lion King

The Monkeys Will Betray You

The Lion King game essentially follows the story of the animated movie, with slight tweaks here and there. Many claim that the hardest part of Westwood Studios' 1994 game based on the Disney flick was the second level, titled "Can't Wait to Be King". The infamous monkey puzzle awaits just beyond what looks like a platform traversal across giraffe heads. It seems simple, but stay with me. Once you jump on the animals' heads—which you'll have to time perfectly, by the way—you reach a group of monkeys meant to pass you around on a tree.

Simba must roar at these monkeys hanging from branches on a tree to change their direction so they can throw Simba over one of the taller giraffes. Specific monkeys wouldn't react to the roar mechanic, while others would. Hit boxes and awkward timing caused this section to drag on and on and on. Many 90s kids rage-quit during this level, learning to accept defeat before it swallowed them whole.

Others pointed to later-game levels that were equally difficult, namely the lava sections plagued with swarms of bats or the "Elephant Graveyard" level featuring annoying hyenas and bone traps that stop players in their tracks.

The 21 Hardest Soulslike RPGs, Ranked By Difficulty

Not all Soulslike on the market can offer the same compelling experience as Dark Souls. Only a few RPGs capture From Soft's rewarding gameplay loop.

By Ritwik Mitra

The co-founder of Westwood Studios, Louis Castle, confirmed in an interview that Disney’s market analytics indicated that players who finished a large portion of the game during a single rental were significantly less likely to purchase the full game after their rental ended. With this in mind, developers were told to alter the game late into production, making portions much harder and others less so. This was done so that Disney could secure sales. 90s kids couldn't finish the game on a rental schedule, typically 6 to 8 hours, so they begged their parents to buy the full game so they could finally taste victory on their own terms.

Contra 3: The Alien Wars

Brain-Breaking Controls & Impossible Death Penalties

Contra 3: The Alien Wars is one of those games that will destroy players if they aren't prepared. I went in with an open mind many years ago and was beaten down so badly that I never picked up the controller again. True story. The game's plot is rather simple, and similar to the other games in the franchise. The run-and-gun action centers around a massive alien invasion in the year 2636 AD. Players must pilot an elite commando tasked with saving mankind from those nasty aliens.

Contra as a series is famously hard, what with its one-hit kill system and the insane enemy waves, but Contra 3: The Alien Wars is a special kind of evil. Levels two and five are especially difficult for me because of the top-down perspective change. Navigating the camera switch while constantly being on the lookout for projectiles while trying to destroy enemy bunkers was insanely hard for younger me, and would likely break my brain as an adult too. During these levels, the character sprite faces forward while players pilot them using the L and R shoulder buttons, which rotate the entire world around you. This mechanic alone was enough to give me a headache.

My least favorite part about this title, and why it was so hard, in my opinion, was the punishing death penalty. Once players eventually (inevitably) die, they will lose all of their equipped artillery in their active slots, including smart bombs. This leaves players wholly unequipped to take on the level again, stripping them bare of all the weapons they might need to progress.

Battletoads In Battlemaniacs

A Whirlwind Ride Without Any Breaks

Battletoads in Battlemaniacs is all about trial and error, which is not something most people are looking for in their gaming experiences. The title is multi-genre, which seems to be the crux of all of the problems pointed out. The game is all about being strategic with resources and learning multiple control schemes to master specific situations the game will throw at you willy-nilly.

Think of this toad-themed game like a punishing gauntlet of sorts. The plot is virtually irrelevant to the gameplay, but, in short, the story follows Rash and Pimple, space toads in a virtual world called The Gamescape tasked with saving fellow toad Zitz from the Dark Queen. Why all the toads are named after skin conditions is still a wonder to me.

New Official SNES Release Confirmed for 2027

A brand-new official release is set to arrive on the Super Nintendo Entertainment System in 2027, and retro game fans won’t want to miss out on it.

By Mohsen Baqery

One minute, players will be in a beat 'em up-style brawl, mashing buttons for their lives, and the next, they're thrown into a tunnel racing level where they must focus on avoiding obstacles. Battletoads in Battlemaniacs is hard because it forces players to adapt on the fly and disrupts their muscle memory with multiple genres. The game's difficulty is only amped up when players realize they only have a set number of lives that begin to dwindle rather quickly, especially on those obstacle-avoiding stages where colliding with a wall causes instant death.

The 7th Saga

A Localization Oopsie That Made A Good Game Bad

The 7th Saga is pretty infamous, mainly for its broken difficulty. This turn-based RPG, which was released in 1993, allows players to choose one of seven warriors to play as in search of runes said to contain exceptional power. The other six warriors who players don't choose immediately become your opposition in search of these runes, helping or hurting you along your journey. Beyond its difficulty, this game is praised for its breathtaking visuals, great soundtrack, and variety of unique playable characters.

The Japanese version of this title, called Elnard , wasn't labeled as particularly difficult, so why is the North American version so punishing? During localization, the game was mistakenly made drastically harder than the Japanese release. This incident became one of the most striking cases of a balancing mishap in JRPG history.

5 Classic NES Games That Hold Up As 10/10 Masterpieces

Most NES games are easy to appreciate but hard to love, but these masterpeices have stood the test of time so well that they still feel perfect.

13
By Mark Sammut

In the US version, stat growth was reduced for player characters, while rival characters and enemies encountered did not share this reduction. It was a huge mathematical misstep. In short, enemies and rivals ended up being way more powerful than player characters, creating a severe disadvantage. This made the game almost literally unbeatable, no matter how hard players may try.

Hagane: The Final Conflict

Crazy Crowded Controls Make Gameplay Difficult

Hagane: The Final Conflict is an action platformer developed by CAProduction. The game is known for being extremely hard to procure, going for thousands of dollars on resale sites, and extremely difficult to play thanks to its complicated controls and combat. Plot-wise, the futuristic game centers around two beefing ninja clans engaged in an all-out war. The Koma clan attacks the Fuma clan, snagging an all-powerful relic in the process. In the Koma clan's wake, the Fuma clan is virtually wiped out, save for a wounded warrior named Hagane. Set on getting revenge, Hagane's broken body and mind are transferred into a ninja robot body.

The Hardest FPS Games Ever Made, Ranked

First-person shooters are a tough genre to get into if someone has never played them before. Some get so hard that they are nearly impossible.

By Charles Burgar

Revenge plots aside, many feel this game is exceedingly difficult because cyborg Hagane has an extremely complex move set that, for the uninitiated, can be very challenging to master. Thrown into a chaotic, fast-paced platforming world with mini-bosses around every corner, players are expected to fight off enemies with an array of weapons that require swapping through while performing moves like wall jumps or directional air-dashes.

Weapons like kunai or grenades feature directional limitations that must be thrown just right, and aerial moves require precision to pull off. It's a lot to put on anyone's plate, especially first-timers. Players often feel like they're overwhelmed with it all, mashing buttons at random to clear a stage. Hagane: The Final Conflict offers little to no direction for said controls, given there is no in-game tutorial that teaches players how to navigate every move set. In short, the title has a lot going on, with little instruction.

Super Star Wars: The Empire Strikes Back

Hoth Is An Icy Hellscape

There are three games in the Super Star Wars series, and all of them are pretty hard. However, Super Star Wars: The Empire Strikes Back seems to be a standout amongst players as the most difficult. This 1993 side-scrolling title is based on the events of the 1980 film of the same name, with tweaks made to make the story more run-and-gun friendly. Essentially, the title consists of massive waves of enemies in familiar locations like Hoth and Dagobah that players are tasked with fighting off. Players can choose to play as either Luke Skywalker, Han Solo, or Chewbacca.

8 Open-World RPGs Perfect For Fans Of Star Wars, Ranked

Need a Star Wars substitute? These open-world RPGs offer gritty, galaxy-spanning sci-fi adventures that hit the same highs as the iconic series.

By Ollie Tuscarny

This game makes you work hard for progress, with waves of enemies coming at you non-stop. Hoth is especially difficult and serves as the setting for most of the early game. The icy wasteland is extremely slippery, and players can go sliding into holes and enemies at random. This, coupled with arbitrary off-screen traps that can and will deal hefty damage, even on easy mode, is a nightmare. All its faults aside, this game does have some great music and a beautiful atmosphere that is a major upgrade on the other two games in the trilogy.

Once players manage to work their way through this painful romp to the end, they're faced with an exceptionally difficult Darth Vader fight plagued by tight corners and strict resource management. In general, bosses in Super Star Wars: The Empire Strikes Back are all quite difficult, largely due to their seemingly infinite health. Many players warned that the only way to beat this game without ripping hair out was with cheats, which seemed to ease the difficulty a bit.

item.title: Final Fantasy 7 Revelation Director Issues New Statement On Physical Copies
item.description:
Final Fantasy 7 Revelation game director Naoki Hamaguchi defended Square Enix's decision to ship the game on discs that require additional data to be downloaded. Final Fantasy 7 Revelation launches on April 8 on all current-gen platforms.

As the climactic bookend of the Final Fantasy 7 Remake series, Final Fantasy 7 Revelation will see the world established by FF7 Remake and Rebirth open up in new ways. As players explore Revelation's landscape, they will eventually battle dangerous Weapon enemies, including the notorious Ruby Weapon and Emerald Weapon. Final Fantasy 7 Revelation will also see the addition of fan-favorite characters Cid and Vincent to the main playable roster, each bringing their own play styles to the fray.

Final Fantasy Game Shadow Dropped for Nintendo Switch 2

Square Enix has announced a new Final Fantasy release for the Nintendo Switch 2 at the recent Nintendo Direct, and it's launching today.

By Drew Swanson

Final Fantasy 7 Revelation Director Discusses Physical Limitations

Despite the excitement around Square Enix's anticipated title, the physical release of Final Fantasy 7 Revelation on PS5 and Xbox has divided fans due to requiring an additional download. In response to these concerns, the Final Fantasy 7 Revelation director stated in an IGN interview that the development team held an internal discussion about what to do with Final Fantasy 7 Revelation 's physical launch. Though some fans pointed out that physical copies of Final Fantasy 7 Rebirth shipped on two discs, Hamaguchi said that the developers chose not to compromise the quality just to get the game to fit on the same disc size as Rebirth . Considering the size and scope of Final Fantasy 7 Revelation 's open world, it is currently unclear if two discs would be sufficient to contain all that the game has to offer. Hamaguchi acknowledged that this decision was not going to meet the expectations of every player.

Though a single Ultra HD Blu-Ray disc can hold up to 100GB of data, the addition of multiple discs within a single game copy also increases the manufacturing costs proportionately. Hamaguchi said that, while the gaming industry in general is pushing toward digital exclusivity, he still saw value in offering a physical edition to gamers who want one. However, Square Enix stated in its Q1 2027 financial results that digital game sales outnumbered physical copies by a margin of nine to one. The gap between physical and digital sales was anchored by Final Fantasy 7 Rebirth 's launch on Switch 2, along with net sales of Final Fantasy 14 ahead of Evercold 's January launch.

However, Final Fantasy 7 Revelation will feature additional content that will necessitate a download in the future. Square Enix previously stated that two FF7 Revelation story expansions focusing on Sephiroth and Vincent will launch between Winter 2027 and April 2028. Between the base game and the planned DLC, it is currently unclear how much storage space Final Fantasy 7 Revelation players must set aside.

Final Fantasy Game Shadow Dropped for Nintendo Switch 2

Given that Final Fantasy 7 Revelation is the end of a long journey that began with the game's first reveal at E3 2015, excitement around Square Enix's blockbuster title remains at a fever pitch. Though FF7 Revelation will also launch digitally on platforms such as Steam, time will tell how many players will still pick up a physical copy of the game.

item.title: Fable Players Are Doubling Down on the Open-World RPG's Most Important Feature
item.description:
From its origins, Fable has been about more than just its story, its combat, and even the quests players take on in their efforts to save the world or assist the citizens of Albion with tasks both mundane and bizarre. Unlike many other RPGs, Fable has been about creating a second life of sorts within a fantasy world where it feels like almost anything is possible—where the choices you make follow you wherever you go and ultimately determine how the road ahead is laid. Yes, its stories have had heart, its characters have had depth, and its combat has had spark, but Fable 's most important feature, the part that truly makes it feel like a fantasy role-playing game, is the life it lets you build in its wonderfully whimsical world. And fans of the upcoming Fable reboot by Playground Games are once again proving that point, as they double down on their previously revealed intentions with the game.

Recently, I wrote an article about a post on Fable 's official X account that invited fans to participate in a sort of survey revolving around what they would spend their hard-earned gold on in the game. After using the comments beneath said X post to form a decent sample, I determined that most players (77% of those who responded to the prompt) are intent on investing heavily in the game's life-sim features—like raising a family, running businesses, and flipping real estate. What made this especially interesting is the controversy around Fable 's confirmed 30–40 hour length, specifically due to the fact that it feels far too short, to some, for an open-world RPG. However, here they are again, doubling down on the side of the aisle where Fable can, according to Playground Games, be played infinitely. That is, the fantasy life-sim portion of the game that has always been at the heart of the franchise.

Fable Is Breaking a Massive Unwritten Rule of Open-World RPGs

Fable is going against one of the biggest expectations surrounding modern open-world RPGs, and the decision could work heavily in its favor.

By Nick Rodriguez

Once Again, Fable Players Prefer the Fantasy Life Over the Heroic Story

Where things get really interesting is that Fable 's official X account recently asked players another question, and this one had almost nothing to do with money. Instead, the account simply asked what the first thing players planned to do once they got to Bowerstone would be. Naturally, there were plenty of answers involving kicking chickens—because this is Fable we're talking about here—but once I started going through the responses, I noticed something very familiar happening. Once again, a huge chunk of players weren't talking about the story, combat, or even questing. They were talking about building a life.

Your Order

More Games

Of the 50 replies in the sample I looked at that actually answered the question being asked, 36 of them, or roughly 72% of those players, leaned toward Fable 's life-sim or sandbox side in some capacity . That includes everything from buying homes and businesses to getting jobs, shopping for clothes, finding a spouse, having children, interacting with NPCs, and generally settling into Bowerstone before worrying too much about whatever grand adventure they've been called to as Albion's new Hero.

Now, obviously, just like the last time I did this, that's still a fairly small sample, and I'm certainly not suggesting 72% of everyone who plays Fable is going to immediately forget the main story exists. But that's also what makes this second sample so interesting to me. The previous post was specifically about what players planned to spend their gold on, so there was at least an argument to be made that the question itself naturally encouraged people to talk about property, businesses, and other parts of the game's life sim. This time, Playground basically handed players a blank check. It asked what they wanted to do first in Bowerstone, and roughly seven out of every 10 relevant responses still ended up somewhere around the life-sim side of the game.

This sample only includes direct replies to Fable 's post that clearly answered the question being asked. Replies that were jokes, reactions, unrelated comments, localization requests, or otherwise didn't indicate what the player planned to do first in Bowerstone were excluded.

Some of those players aren't exactly hiding their priorities, either. User @ArtemisOdinson said they plan to get a job and buy every building available before "the story can continue." User @Germis34954388 said they intend to do "everything except quest or story." User @TheAgentShark apparently wants to find a blacksmith, get a job, find a chicken, and kick it, which is about as efficient a summary of the Fable experience as I could probably come up with. And there are plenty of other players in the comments who say they're already planning their marriages, their families, their property empires, their wardrobes, and even which parts of Bowerstone they want to memorize before they've spent a single minute actually playing the game.

And again, that's almost exactly what happened the last time Fable asked its community a question like this. That first sample landed at 77% of relevant replies pointing toward the life-sim or sandbox portion of the game. This one landed at 72%. Two different questions, two different sets of responses, and both of them have roughly three-quarters of the players answering in a way that suggests being a Hero might not always be at the top of their list.

Fable's Life Sim Is Starting to Look Like the Main Event

In other words, that's why I don't really see Fable 's life systems as some collection of side activities designed to keep players busy between quests. They may technically exist outside the main story, but at this point, fans are repeatedly showing that what is arguably Fable 's most important feature is one of the main reasons they want to play the game in the first place. I say it's the most important feature, because it's one of the main things that sets Fable apart from other RPGs, not just because it lets players do one thing or another, but because they can essentially do it all. Even games like Skyrim that let players purchase a home don't allow the kind of open sandbox that Fable offers, and players are already proving that they're here for it.

In fact, only one of the 50 relevant replies in this latest sample explicitly said the first thing they planned to do was complete the story. Again, I'm not taking that to mean players don't care about Fable 's story, because that would obviously be ridiculous. But I do think it says something about what people picture when they imagine themselves stepping into Albion. Rather than only imagining themselves as the Hero, they're imagining who they're going to marry, where they're going to live, what they're going to own, how they're going to make money, and what kind of completely unnecessary trouble they're going to get into along the way.

Fable Players Are Doubling Down on the Open-World RPG's Most Important Feature
February 2027 is Already a Super Busy Month for Gamers
Fable Players Are Already Proving Playground Right About the Open-World RPG's Length
Fable Is Treating NPCs the Way More Open-World RPGs Should

That's what Fable has always done differently, and Playground seems to understand that. The main story will eventually end, and the quests will eventually run dry. Albion itself, though, is being built around the franchise's best feature—one that can apparently keep going for as long as players are willing to mess with them. Based on two completely separate samples now, a lot of Fable players seem more than willing.

In other words, that's why I don't really see Fable 's life systems as some collection of side activities designed to keep players busy between quests. They may technically exist outside the main story, but at this point, fans are repeatedly showing that what is arguably Fable 's most important feature is one of the main reasons they want to play the game in the first place. I say it's the most important feature, because it's one of the main things that sets Fable apart from other RPGs, not just because it lets players do one thing or another, but because they can essentially do it all. Even games like Skyrim that let players purchase a home don't allow the kind of open sandbox that Fable offers, and players are already proving that they're here for it.

In fact, only one of the 50 relevant replies in this latest sample explicitly said the first thing they planned to do was complete the story. Again, I'm not taking that to mean players don't care about Fable 's story, because that would obviously be ridiculous. But I do think it says something about what people picture when they imagine themselves stepping into Albion. Rather than only imagining themselves as the Hero, they're imagining who they're going to marry, where they're going to live, what they're going to own, how they're going to make money, and what kind of completely unnecessary trouble they're going to get into along the way.

Fable Players Are Doubling Down on the Open-World RPG's Most Important Feature
February 2027 is Already a Super Busy Month for Gamers
Fable Players Are Already Proving Playground Right About the Open-World RPG's Length
Fable Is Treating NPCs the Way More Open-World RPGs Should

That's what Fable has always done differently, and Playground seems to understand that. The main story will eventually end, and the quests will eventually run dry. Albion itself, though, is being built around the franchise's best feature—one that can apparently keep going for as long as players are willing to mess with them. Based on two completely separate samples now, a lot of Fable players seem more than willing.

You can travel through different areas, look for clues, and keep searching until you find what you're after. The promo codes provide useful rewards to help along the way. You can get Gems and Alien Coins, giving you extra resources to spend as you continue exploring and searching.
